front: What distinguishes a contactor from an ordinary control relay?
back: A contactor is a relay with a high power rating, designed to be connected directly to high-current loads such as electric motors.
excerpt: Unlike other relays, contactors are designed to be directly connected to high-current load devices.

front: What does a direct on line (DOL) motor starter do when it is energised?
back: It immediately connects the motor terminals directly to the power supply, applying the full line voltage at once.
excerpt: When energized, a direct on line (DOL) starter immediately connects the motor terminals directly to the power supply.
mnemonic: DOL = Direct On Line: the motor goes straight onto the supply line, nothing in between.

front: Why does a motor on a magnetic-contactor starter stay off when power returns after a failure?
back: Losing voltage drops the contactor out, opening the auxiliary contact that held its coil energised; it closes again only on a new start command.
excerpt: If a momentary loss of supply voltage occurs, the contactor will open and not close again until a new start command is given.

front: How does a thermal overload relay stop an overloaded motor?
back: Motor current heats a bimetallic strip; in an overload it bends until it pushes a trip bar that cuts power to the contactor coil.
excerpt: The hotter the strip, the more it deflects to the point it pushes a trip bar which disconnects power to the contactor solenoid, turning everything off.
mnemonic: Overcurrent → heat → bimetal bends → trip bar → contactor coil off.

front: Why does a thermal overload relay not trip on a motor's brief, high starting current?
back: Its heater and bimetallic strip need time to warm up, and that delay lets the motor start and settle to normal running current.
excerpt: The heater coil and the action of the bi-metallic strip introduce a time delay that affords the motor time to start and settle into normal running current without the thermal overload tripping.

front: Why are larger motors started with reduced-voltage starters instead of direct on line?
back: To reduce the high inrush current of starting, which would otherwise cause voltage dips on the power supply.
excerpt: To reduce the inrush current, larger motors will have reduced-voltage starters or adjustable-speed drives in order to minimise voltage dips to the power supply.

front: How does a reversing starter make a three-phase motor turn the other way?
back: It swaps the wires connecting any two of the three phases.
excerpt: For three phase motors, this is achieved by swapping the wires connecting any two phases.

front: Which property of the supply to an alternating-current (AC) motor does a speed controller vary to change its speed?
back: The frequency of the alternating current applied to the motor, which power electronic devices adjust.
excerpt: change the frequency of the AC applied to the motor for speed control using power electronic devices

front: In a control loop, what is the final control element?
back: The device that acts on the process itself, such as a control valve, damper, motor or solenoid valve, closing the loop with the measuring instrument and controller.
excerpt: The control of parameters of a system is achieved in the final control element which forms a closed loop along with measuring instrument and control system.

back: A machine component that produces force, torque or displacement when it is supplied with an electrical, pneumatic or hydraulic input.
excerpt: An actuator is a component of a machine that produces force, torque, or displacement, when an electrical, pneumatic or hydraulic input is supplied to it
mnemonic: Sensors feel, actuators move: an actuator is a 'mover'.

front: How does a double-acting cylinder differ from a single-acting one?
back: Fluid pressure drives its piston in both directions; a single-acting cylinder is pressure-driven one way only and returns by a spring, gravity or another force.
excerpt: In a double acting actuator, the return stroke is driven by fluid pressure applied to the opposite side of the piston.

front: Why can a hydraulic actuator exert a large force?
back: It is driven by a pressurised liquid, and liquids are nearly impossible to compress.
excerpt: Since liquids are nearly impossible to compress, a hydraulic actuator can exert a large force.
